chapter.name: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments

questions.q: What does the chapter call the creation of rules by a government?
questions.a: The legislative function

questions.q: In the same week the Union Government (1) holds talks with a neighbouring country on sharing the water of a river that flows through both, and (2) changes the rules on how much interest banks may charge on loans to small traders. Which pair of roles of government from the chapter's list do these two actions show, in order?
questions.a: Managing relationships with other countries; managing the economy and economic activities
o: Managing relationships with other countries; managing the economy and economic activities
Taking care of national defence; managing the economy and economic activities
Managing relationships with other countries; delivering essential goods and services
Taking care of national defence; working for the welfare and improving people's lives

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the school example, the third method of forming the Student Committee is called a democratic way of forming a committee.
Reason (R): In the third method, the students of each grade choose one representative from among themselves through voting.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) What does the word 'representative' mean, as the chapter defines it?
(b) In the school example, who would sit on the Student Committee under the third method?
questions.a: (a) A person who is chosen to act or make decisions on behalf of another person or group of people. (b) One representative from each grade, chosen by the students of that grade through voting.
s: (a) A person chosen to act or make decisions on behalf of another person or group
(b) One representative from each grade, chosen by that grade's students through voting

questions.q: True or False: In the school example, the chapter finds that making every student of the school a member of the committee is the most effective method. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: False. If every student is part of the committee, it will be difficult to reach decisions and manage implementation; the chapter calls the third method, where each grade elects a representative, the democratic way.
s: States the verdict: False
Reason: with everyone on the committee it is difficult to reach decisions and manage implementation

questions.q: Name the three functions of government described in the chapter, and state in one line what each function does.
questions.a: Legislative function: creating the rules that serve as the framework for running the country. Executive function: implementing these rules and administering the country according to them. Judicial function: ensuring that the rules are followed.
s: Legislative function: creating rules (framework for running the country)
Executive function: implementing the rules and administering the country by them
Judicial function: ensuring that the rules are followed

questions.q:
Three things happen in Indore about plastic bags.
(i) The city council passes a rule that shops may not give out plastic bags.
(ii) City officers visit the markets and take away the plastic bags still kept in shops.
(iii) A shopkeeper who was fined says the fine is unfair; a court hears both sides and decides whether he broke the rule.
Name the function of government that each step shows, and give a reason for each.
questions.a: (i) Legislative function, because a rule is being created. (ii) Executive function, because the rule is being implemented. (iii) Judicial function, because the court is ensuring that the rule is followed by deciding whether it was broken.
s: (i) Legislative: a rule is created
(ii) Executive: the rule is implemented
(iii) Judicial: the court ensures the rule is followed by deciding the dispute

questions.q:
The chapter opens with Kautilya's words: a ruler's duties are raksha (protection of the state from external aggression), palana (maintenance of law and order within the state) and yogakshema (safeguarding the welfare of the people). In one month a state government (P) posts extra soldiers along the border, (Q) opens new police stations in two towns, and (R) starts free check-ups in its hospitals. Meera says, 'Kautilya's three duties are just another name for the chapter's three functions of government.'
(a) Match each of P, Q and R to Kautilya's duty it serves.
(b) Is Meera right? Explain the difference between Kautilya's duties and the chapter's three functions.
(c) Show how all three functions of government are needed to carry out palana, using one law as your example.
(d) Kautilya was writing for a ruler. Using the school example, explain who decides in a democracy which people will carry out these duties.
questions.a: (a) P: raksha; Q: palana; R: yogakshema. (b) No. Kautilya's duties name WHAT a government must look after (security, law and order, welfare), and they match roles in the chapter's list such as national defence, law and order and welfare. The three functions describe HOW any task is done: making rules (legislative), implementing them (executive) and ensuring they are followed (judicial). (c) For example, a law against stealing: the legislature makes the rule (legislative), the police and administration enforce it (executive), and the courts decide when it has been broken (judicial). Without any one of these, law and order cannot be maintained. (d) As in the third method of the school example, where each grade elects its representative, in a democracy the people select their representatives to govern them, so the people decide who carries out these duties.
s: (a) P raksha, Q palana, R yogakshema
(b) Not right: duties are roles/goals (what), functions are make, implement, ensure rules are followed (how)
(c) One law shown through legislative, executive and judicial functions
(d) The people elect representatives, as the students elect one per grade

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer.
The girls of a hostel in Shillong live on five floors and come from many different states. The warden says the hostel mess needs a committee. Some senior girls say that they alone should plan the menu. Lalremsiami, a first-year girl, says that the seniors would not know what the girls on the other floors need. Another girl suggests that all the girls of the hostel should sit on the committee, but the warden says that would make decisions very slow. In the end, the girls of each floor vote to choose one girl to speak for them. The committee then writes a new rule: one dish from a different state will be served every week.
(a) What does the chapter call a person, like each chosen girl, who acts or makes decisions on behalf of a group?
(b) Which problem does Lalremsiami point out in letting only the seniors decide?
(c) Why does the chapter's school example also reject the idea of everyone joining the committee?
(d) Writing the new menu rule is like which function of government?
questions.a: (a) A representative. (b) A group of only some students would not know the problems and needs of the others, so their voices would not be heard. (c) If everyone is on the committee, it is difficult to reach decisions and to manage implementation effectively. (d) The legislative function, which is the creation of rules.
s: (a) Representative
(b) The seniors alone would not know the needs and problems of the others
(c) With everyone on it, it is hard to reach decisions and manage implementation
(d) Legislative function (creating rules)

questions.q: According to the chapter, what is the source of a government's authority in a theocracy?
questions.a: Religious beliefs and the head of a religious institution
o: Religious beliefs and the head of a religious institution
The people of the country, through elections held at fixed intervals
The royal family, through birth of the eldest son into the family
A small group of wealthy and influential families of the country

questions.q:
Read these statements about the principles of democracy.
I. Universal adult franchise means the right to vote in elections for all adults.
II. An independent judiciary makes sure that the citizens follow the laws, but it cannot check the parts of the government.
III. The chapter says that not all democracies are able to put the fundamental principles into practice.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the principle of democracy it shows in Column B.
Column A: 1. A rich trader and a daily-wage worker get the same punishment for the same offence  2. A college student writes to a newspaper disagreeing with a new rule of the state government  3. The voters of Wardha choose their member of the legislature in an election  4. A court orders a government department to stop breaking a law
Column B: A. Freedom  B. Independent judiciary  C. Equality  D. Representative participation

(a) What is a 'constitution', as the chapter describes it?
(b) In a monarchy, who decides how the government will work?
questions.a: (a) A book of the fundamental rules of a country, in which the system that decides how the government will work is written down. (b) The king or queen.
s: (a) A book of the fundamental rules of the country that sets how the government works
(b) The king or queen

questions.q: True or False: India gave the right to vote to all adults from the very beginning of the Indian republic in 1950. Give a fact from the chapter that supports your answer.
questions.a: True. The chapter says India provided universal adult franchise from the very beginning of the Indian republic in 1950, while in Switzerland women got the right to vote only in 1971.
s: States the verdict: True
Supporting fact: universal adult franchise from the start of the republic in 1950 (unlike Switzerland, 1971)

questions.q:
The chapter names three fundamental rights that a democracy protects: the right to equality, the right to freedom of speech and expression, and the right against exploitation. Name the right that is broken in each case.
(i) The owner of a brick kiln makes workers labour 14 hours a day and pays them nothing.
(ii) A folk singer is jailed for a song that makes fun of a minister.
(iii) A police station registers complaints from rich families but turns poor families away.
questions.a: (i) The right against exploitation. (ii) The right to freedom of speech and expression. (iii) The right to equality, since everyone should be equal before the law.
s: (i) Right against exploitation
(ii) Right to freedom of speech and expression
(iii) Right to equality (equal before the law)

questions.q:
Answer these questions on the fundamental principles of democracy.
(a) Apart from being equal before the law, what else does equality in a democracy mean?
(b) What does freedom in a democracy mean?
(c) Through which process do people choose their representatives, and which body do the elected representatives become part of?
(d) What is meant by universal adult franchise?
(e) A government office stops a citizen from speaking freely about its work. Which part of a democracy ensures that her fundamental rights are protected?
questions.a: (a) Every person has the right to be treated equally and to have equal access to facilities like education and health. (b) Citizens have the right to make their own choices and express their opinions. (c) Through elections; the elected representatives become part of the legislature. (d) The right to vote in elections for all adults, that is, every citizen above a certain age. (e) The independent judiciary.
s: (a) Right to be treated equally and equal access to education and health
(b) Right to make own choices and express opinions
(c) Elections; representatives join the legislature
(d) Right to vote for all adults (every citizen above a certain age)
(e) The independent judiciary

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Two governments can both have legislative, executive and judicial functions and still be organised very differently.
Reason (R): The three functions of government can be performed by totally independent bodies or by the same body.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: How often are general elections held in India, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Every five years

questions.q: What is the Lower House of India's Parliament called?
questions.a: Lok Sabha

questions.q: In the country of Melora, the voters choose the head of the executive in a separate vote of their own, and none of the ministers sits in the legislature. Which form of government does Melora have?
questions.a: A presidential democracy

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with its meaning in Column B.
Column A: 1. Executive  2. Legislature  3. Separation of power  4. Accountability
Column B: A. The body of government responsible for making laws  B. The government is answerable to the people who elected it  C. The organ of government responsible for implementing the law  D. The three organs work independently and do not interfere in each other's functions

Assertion (A): In India, the voters choose the prime minister directly in a separate vote.
Reason (R): In a parliamentary democracy, people elect the legislature, and selected members of the legislature become ministers.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
(a) What does accountability mean in a democracy?
(b) Why are elections in a representative democracy held at regular and fixed intervals?
questions.a: (a) The government is answerable to the people who have elected it. (b) So that people can express changes in their choices, and replace their representatives if they wish; this keeps the government accountable to them.
s: (a) The government is answerable to the people who elected it
(b) So that people can express changes in their choices (and keep the government accountable)

questions.q: True or False: In most countries, the Upper House of the legislature is always formed by election, and it is more powerful than the Lower House. Give the correct position from the chapter.
questions.a: False. The Upper House is formed either by election or by nomination, and it is the Lower House, elected by direct voting, that is generally more powerful than the Upper House.
s: States the verdict: False
Correction: the Upper House is formed by election or nomination; the Lower House is generally more powerful

questions.q:
The chapter's table gives the year democracy was established in six countries: USA 1787, Switzerland 1848, India 1947, Germany 1949, Kenya 1964, Nepal 2008.
(i) Arrange the six countries in order, earliest first.
(ii) Name the countries in the table that became democracies after India.
(iii) Explain, using the chapter, why the year a country became a democracy does not by itself tell us that it had every principle of democracy from that year.
questions.a: (i) USA (1787), Switzerland (1848), India (1947), Germany (1949), Kenya (1964), Nepal (2008). (ii) Germany, Kenya and Nepal. (iii) Democracies have evolved over time: when countries adopted democracy they may not have had all the principles of democracy as we understand them today, for example universal adult suffrage came later in some of them.
s: (i) USA, Switzerland, India, Germany, Kenya, Nepal
(ii) Germany, Kenya, Nepal
(iii) Democracies evolve; countries may not have had all principles when they adopted democracy

questions.q:
Marovia is a representative democracy. Its voters elect the 240 members of its legislature, the National Council, at a fixed interval of five years. The head of the executive, Chief Minister Aren Tal, and her 18 ministers are all members of the National Council, and the voters did not vote for them separately as ministers. In March 2026, 131 of the 240 members voted that they no longer had confidence in the ministers, and all the ministers resigned. A week later, Marovia's highest court cancelled an order given by a minister because it broke a law, and the ministers obeyed the court.
(a) Is Marovia a parliamentary or a presidential democracy? Give two facts from the passage that settle it.
(b) Did more than half of the members vote against the ministers? Show your working.
(c) Which idea from the chapter does the court's action show? Explain in one line.
(d) No court and no election forced the ministers to resign. What does their resignation show about to whom the ministers are accountable, and how does this keep the government accountable to the people?
questions.a: (a) Parliamentary: the ministers are also members of the legislature, the people elected the legislature but not the executive, and the ministers continued only while they had the confidence of the legislature (they resigned when they lost it). (b) Yes: half of 240 is 120, and 131 is more than 120 (131/240 is about 54.6%). (c) Separation of power, with an independent judiciary: the court works independently of the executive and makes sure all parts of the government follow the laws. (d) The ministers are accountable to the legislature and can continue only while they have its confidence; since the people elect the legislature, the government stays answerable to the people through it.
s: (a) Parliamentary, with two facts: ministers are members of the legislature / people did not elect the executive / ministers resigned on losing confidence
(b) Half of 240 = 120; 131 > 120, so yes (about 54.6%)
(c) Separation of power / independent judiciary: laws are followed by all parts of the government
(d) Ministers are accountable to the legislature (need its confidence); the legislature is elected by the people

questions.q: To which period and century do the Uttaramerur inscriptions in Tamil Nadu belong?
questions.a: The Chola period, 10th century CE

questions.q: A historian lists four features of ancient states. Which one could ALSO be true of a mahajanapada headed by a king, and so does NOT by itself show that a state was an early republic?
questions.a: Its ruler took the advice of a sabha or samiti seriously.
o: Its ruler took the advice of a sabha or samiti seriously.
Its leaders were chosen on the basis of merit rather than birth.
Its key positions were filled through elections.
Its head of state was elected and was not a hereditary monarch.

questions.q:
Read these statements about republics in history.
I. In the Vajji mahajanapada, leaders were chosen by birth from among the Lichchhavi clan.
II. A republic is a form of government in which the head of state is elected and is not a hereditary monarch.
III. According to the Uttaramerur inscriptions, a member of the village sabha found to have indulged in corruption would be removed immediately.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q:
(a) What did staying within the limits of rajadharma mean for a king?
(b) Name the text, and its author, that tells the story of King Chandrapida and the cobbler.
questions.a: (a) Ruling according to dharma and ensuring the welfare of all people. (b) The Rajatarangini, by the Kashmiri scholar Kalhana (12th century CE).
s: (a) Ruling according to dharma and ensuring the welfare of all people
(b) Rajatarangini by Kalhana

questions.q: True or False: The Uttaramerur inscriptions show that members of a local body were chosen by election even in a period when power was in the hands of a king. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: True. The inscriptions, from the Chola period (10th century CE), describe the election of members to the village sabha, a local administrative body; the chapter uses them to show that the voice of the common people was valued even when power was in the hands of a king or queen.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: Chola-period inscriptions describe elections to the village sabha under a king

questions.q: Give any three details about the village sabha elections that we learn from the Uttaramerur inscriptions.
questions.a: Any three of: the election process used sealed ballot boxes; the inscriptions list the qualifications of members; they set out the members' duties; they give the conditions that could lead to a member's dismissal, for example immediate removal for corruption.
s: First detail (e.g. sealed ballot boxes)
Second detail (e.g. qualifications of members, or their duties)
Third detail (e.g. conditions for dismissal, such as removal for corruption)

questions.q:
The chapter describes three ways in which people holding power were checked in early India: (1) under the Uttaramerur inscriptions, a member of the village sabha found to have indulged in corruption would be removed immediately; (2) a king was expected to stay within the limits of rajadharma; (3) in the Vajji mahajanapada, decisions were taken collectively by representatives of various clans.
(i) Which of these checks states a definite consequence for the person who breaks it?
(ii) What does the chapter say about how far kings actually kept to check (2)?
(iii) Decide which of checks (1) and (2) was the surer limit on a person in power, and justify your decision from (i) and (ii).
questions.a: (i) Check (1): a corrupt member would be removed immediately. (ii) Rajadharma was an ideal that kings did not necessarily achieve, and some kings used their power to subjugate their people. (iii) Check (1) was the surer limit: it named a definite consequence (immediate removal) that applied to every member, whereas check (2) depended on the king himself choosing to follow an ideal, with no stated consequence if he did not.
s: (i) Check (1): immediate removal for corruption
(ii) Rajadharma was an ideal kings did not necessarily achieve
(iii) Check (1), because it carried a definite consequence while (2) relied on the king's own choice

questions.q:
The chapter says: 'The voice of the common people has been valued and upheld in India through the ages, even when the power was in the hands of a king or queen.' Evaluate this statement.
(a) Give evidence from the Vajji mahajanapada.
(b) Give evidence from the Uttaramerur inscriptions.
(c) Explain how the sabha or samiti and rajadharma were meant to limit kings.
(d) Give the chapter's own caution that shows this ideal was not always met.
(e) Give your overall judgement on the statement.
questions.a: (a) In Vajji the Lichchhavi clan practised collective decision-making, leaders were chosen on merit, key positions were filled through elections and representatives of various clans met regularly to address issues for the people's welfare. (b) The 10th-century CE Chola-period inscriptions describe elections to the village sabha with sealed ballot boxes, qualifications, duties and dismissal, for example immediate removal for corruption. (c) Mahajanapada kings were guided by the sabha or samiti and expected to take their advice seriously; under rajadharma a king had to rule by dharma for the welfare of all, as Chandrapida did by asking the cobbler's permission and paying him. (d) The chapter says rajadharma was an ideal that kings did not necessarily achieve, and that some kings used their power to subjugate their people. (e) The statement is largely supported by the evidence, but it describes an ideal and a tradition, not something every king followed.
s: (a) Vajji: collective decisions, merit, elections, clan representatives
(b) Uttaramerur: elections to the village sabha with ballot boxes, qualifications, dismissal
(c) Sabha/samiti advice and rajadharma (welfare of all), with an example
(d) Caution: an ideal not always achieved; some kings subjugated their people
(e) Judgement: largely supported, but an ideal rather than a rule every king followed

questions.a: The prime minister, leading the Council of Ministers

The king or queen, as the head of the state and its monarch

A case is judged by someone when there is a dispute between people.
People in a place are brought under control by force and made to obey.

Reason (R): Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy, in which the king holds all power and governs according to Islamic law.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Match each description in Column A with the country the chapter uses as its example in Column B.
Column A: 1. The king holds all power and is not bound by the advice of the council he appoints  2. The monarch has only nominal power, and the elected parliament makes all the laws  3. A Supreme Leader selected by clerics for life has authority over an elected president and parliament  4. A republic with a prime minister and council of ministers who are also members of Parliament
Column B: A. United Kingdom  B. India  C. Saudi Arabia  D. Iran
True or False: In Iran, the Supreme Leader is elected by all the citizens for a fixed term. Give the correct position from the chapter.
questions.a: False. The Supreme Leader is selected by a group of Islamic clerics and his term is for life; it is the president and the parliament that are elected and take care of everyday governance.
s: States the verdict: False
Correction: selected by Islamic clerics, for life (the president and parliament are elected)

questions.q:
(a) What is a theocracy?
(b) Apart from Iran, name two theocracies that exist today, according to the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A form of government where the country is ruled by the rules of religion and religious leaders. (b) Afghanistan and Vatican City.
s: (a) Ruled by the rules of religion and religious leaders
(b) Afghanistan and Vatican City

questions.q: A student writes: 'A country can be called sovereign only if a king or queen rules it. A theocracy is a country where a king makes all the laws by himself, and Afghanistan is the chapter's example of such an absolute monarchy.' Point out three errors in this statement, using the chapter.
questions.a: (1) Sovereign indicates that the source of power of a country is independent from external influence; it does not require a king or queen. (2) A theocracy is ruled by the rules of religion and religious leaders; a monarch who has complete control over making laws describes an absolute monarchy, not a theocracy. (3) The chapter names Afghanistan as a theocracy; its example of an absolute monarchy is Saudi Arabia.
s: Error 1: sovereign means the source of power is independent from external influence, not rule by a monarch
Error 2: a theocracy is ruled by the rules of religion and religious leaders, not a law-making king
Error 3: Afghanistan is a theocracy; the absolute monarchy example is Saudi Arabia

questions.q:
Varna is a fictional kingdom today. King Arun inherited the throne from his father. He makes the laws, his officers make sure they are followed, and he himself settles disputes when they are not. He has appointed a 15-member council. Last year the council advised him on 10 matters: he followed its advice on 6 and rejected it on 4. A newspaper in Varna writes, 'The king's power is limited, because he has a council.'
(a) Which of the chapter's three functions of government does Arun hold?
(b) What does last year's record show about the council's advice? Use the numbers.
(c) Decide whether the newspaper is right, name the type of monarchy Varna is, and give the chapter's example of it.
(d) Give one way in which the ideal expected of kings in many parts of early India limited them, which Arun's arrangement does not.
questions.a: (a) All three: legislative (making laws), executive (enforcing them) and judicial (adjudicating disputes). (b) He rejected the council's advice on 4 of 10 matters (40%), so its advice does not bind him; he follows it only when he chooses. (c) The newspaper is wrong: a council whose advice the king may reject does not limit him. Varna is an absolute monarchy, like Saudi Arabia, where the king holds all power and appoints a council but is not bound by its advice. (d) Those kings were expected to stay within the limits of rajadharma (ruling according to dharma and ensuring the welfare of all), and to take the advice of the sabha or samiti seriously; Arun has no such expectation on him and can set aside his council.
s: (a) Legislative, executive and judicial functions
(b) Rejected 4 of 10, so the advice is not binding
(c) Newspaper wrong; absolute monarchy; Saudi Arabia
(d) Rajadharma / taking the sabha or samiti's advice seriously

questions.q: In which year was Adolf Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany?

questions.a: Rule by a few

questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
(a) What is known as the 'Holocaust', according to the chapter?
(b) In which years was World War II fought?
questions.a: (a) The killing of at least six million Jews, for which Adolf Hitler was responsible. (b) 1939 to 1945.

questions.q:
The chapter mentions the Roma people in its account of dictatorship. Answer.
(i) Under which dictator were hundreds of thousands of Roma killed?
(ii) What way of life did the Roma originally follow?
(iii) Where do scholars say the Roma originated, and on what basis?
questions.a: (i) Adolf Hitler, who was responsible for the killing of six million Jews as well as hundreds of thousands of Roma and other groups. (ii) They were originally nomads. (iii) In India, on the basis of their linguistic and cultural characteristics.
s: (i) Adolf Hitler
(ii) Nomads
(iii) India, from their linguistic and cultural characteristics

questions.q:
Say whether each country is a dictatorship, an oligarchy, or neither of the two. Give one reason from the chapter for each.
(i) In Kalpa, a king is the head of state, but an elected parliament makes all the laws and a prime minister heads the executive.
(ii) In Vardesh, a prime minister closes the parliament, sets aside the constitution and passes orders that no law can limit.
(iii) In an ancient city-state, a handful of aristocratic families take every important decision for all the people.
questions.a: (i) Neither: it is a constitutional monarchy, really a parliamentary democracy, since the elected parliament makes the laws and the king has only nominal power. (ii) Dictatorship: one person possesses absolute power with no limits imposed by a constitution or law. (iii) Oligarchy: a small, powerful group, here aristocratic families, makes all the important decisions, as in some places in ancient Greece.
s: (i) Neither: constitutional monarchy, the elected parliament makes the laws
(ii) Dictatorship: absolute power with no limits from a constitution or law
(iii) Oligarchy: a small group of aristocratic families makes the decisions

questions.q:
Tarvania calls itself a republic and holds a vote for its president every five years. In 2015, 2020 and 2025 there was only one name on the ballot, the same ruler's, and he got 99% of the votes each time. In 2016 he passed laws that banned every other political party. Since then the parliament has met only to approve, without change, the laws his office writes, and his own officers carry those laws out.
(a) The chapter defines a republic as a government whose head of state is elected and is not a hereditary monarch. Does Tarvania's ruler fit the words of this definition? Why?
(b) The chapter says every person has the right to choose and elect their representatives. Which principle of democracy does it call this, and why is it missing when the voters have only one name to choose from?
(c) Which feature of democratic government is missing when the parliament only approves the laws the ruler's office writes?
(d) Decide whether Tarvania is really a democracy or a dictatorship, and justify your decision with the chapter's definition.
questions.a: (a) Only on paper: he comes to office through a vote and does not inherit the throne, so the words fit, but the vote offers no real choice. (b) Representative participation; with only one name on the ballot the voters cannot choose between representatives, so the right exists only on paper. (c) Separation of power: the legislature does not work independently of the executive, because the ruler's office both writes the laws and carries them out. (d) A dictatorship: one person possesses absolute power with no real limits, since the other parties are banned and the parliament cannot refuse his laws; the one-name vote does not make it a democracy.
s: (a) Fits the words only on paper: chosen by a vote, not hereditary, but no real choice
(b) Representative participation, with the reason that one name gives no real choice
(c) Separation of power: the legislature does not work independently of the executive
(d) Dictatorship: one person holds absolute power, justified with the data

questions.q:
Selvia is a fictional country. Read its record.
2015: Selvia elects its parliament; newspapers are free and the courts are independent.
2019: Four wealthy business families fund almost every minister, and the important decisions of the government are first settled at their meetings, though elections still take place.
2022: President Doran passes laws that give him full power and ban all other parties; no constitution or law now limits what he does.
(a) In which year does Selvia first show signs of oligarchy? Give the reason from the chapter.
(b) In which year does Selvia become a dictatorship? Give the reason from the chapter's definition.
(c) Compare 2019 and 2022: who holds power in each?
(d) Name one principle of democracy that citizens lose in 2022 that they still had in 2019, and say why.
(e) Decide which situation, 2019 or 2022, would be harder for ordinary citizens to correct through elections, and justify.
questions.a: (a) 2019: a small group of wealthy business families holds too much influence in governance, which political commentators call a sign of oligarchy even in a democracy. (b) 2022: one person now possesses absolute power and has no limits imposed by a constitution or law. (c) In 2019 a small, powerful group of wealthy families makes the important decisions; in 2022 one person, President Doran, holds all the power. (d) Representative participation (or freedom): with all other parties banned, people can no longer choose between representatives, as they still could in 2019. (e) 2022 is harder: in 2019 elections were still held, so people could change their representatives and keep a check on the government, but in 2022 other parties are banned and no law limits the ruler, so elections can no longer change the government.
s: (a) 2019; a small group of wealthy people holds too much influence
(b) 2022; one person with absolute power, no limits from constitution or law
(c) 2019 a few families; 2022 one person
(d) A principle lost in 2022 (e.g. representative participation), with reason
(e) 2022, because elections no longer offer a way to change the government

questions.q: According to the chapter, what share of the world's countries have adopted democracy and democratic forms of government?
questions.a: More than half of them
o: Fewer than a quarter of them

questions.q: In a democracy, the voters of a state replaced their government at the last election because it had failed to supply clean drinking water. The new government's ministers now say, 'If we fail too, we will be voted out next time.' Which idea from the chapter does their remark show?
questions.a: Elections keep a constant check on what a democratic government does.
o: Elections keep a constant check on what a democratic government does.
Separation of power keeps the judiciary independent of the executive.
In a direct democracy the citizens take every decision themselves.
Freedom lets people choose what to speak, wear and believe.

questions.q:
Read these statements about the hurdles that democracies face, according to the chapter.
I. Corruption can cause hurdles in achieving the ideals of democracy.
II. Erosion of the judiciary's independence is one of the issues the chapter names.
III. Wealth equality among citizens is named as one of the hurdles.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In most countries, democracy is considered to be a better form of government than others.
Reason (R): More than half of the countries in the world have adopted democracy and democratic forms of government.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) Name any two issues that, according to the chapter, can cause hurdles in achieving the ideals of democracy.
(b) In a democracy, what can the people do if the government does not perform its functions properly?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: corruption, wealth disparity, excessive control by a few over democratic institutions, erosion of the judiciary's independence, manipulation of information channels. (b) They can change their representatives through elections.
s: (a) Any two hurdles named in the chapter (e.g. corruption, wealth disparity)
(b) Change their representatives through elections

questions.q:
In Table 9.2 the chapter has already filled 'No' for universal adult franchise in a dictatorship. Fill the dictatorship column for the three rows below with Yes or No, and give a reason from the chapter for each.
(i) Freedom of speech
(ii) Separation of powers
(iii) Equality amongst citizens
questions.a: (i) No: a dictator has absolute power and can silence people; Hitler eliminated the opposition, and in Shane's country the government watches every action. (ii) No: one person or a small group holds absolute power, so the legislature, executive and judiciary do not work independently of the ruler. (iii) No: Hitler treated some peoples as 'inferior races' and was responsible for killing at least six million Jews, and under Idi Amin many Indians were forced to flee Uganda.
s: (i) No, with a reason (e.g. opposition eliminated, every action watched)
(ii) No: absolute power in one person or group, organs not independent
(iii) No, with a reason (e.g. Hitler's 'inferior races', Indians forced out of Uganda)

questions.q:
Ananya lives in Pune, in a democracy. The chapter describes the everyday choices that people in a genuine democracy can make for themselves.
(a) Name two things from the chapter that Ananya can choose for herself.
(b) Give one example from a school day of Ananya using one of these choices.
(c) State the limit that the chapter places on these choices.
(d) Her neighbour plays loud music on speakers at 2 a.m. every night and says, 'It is my freedom.' Using the limit, say whether this is protected.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: what to speak, what to wear, what beliefs to follow, how to express herself. (b) Any fitting example, such as giving her own opinion in a class debate or wearing the clothes she likes to a school function. (c) These choices can be made only until and unless they harm someone else's rights. (d) It is not protected, because it harms the neighbours' rights, such as their right to rest at night.
s: (a) Two choices: what to speak, wear, believe, or how to express herself
(b) A fitting school-day example of one choice
(c) The limit: only until it harms someone else's rights
(d) Not protected, because it harms the neighbours' rights

questions.q:
Class 7B of a school in Bhopal has 36 students sitting in 6 rows of 6. They act out three forms of government in a role play.
Round 1: Arjun becomes 'king' because his 'father', the old king, has died, and he alone makes every class rule.
Round 2: Riya grabs the class register, declares herself ruler and bans anyone from speaking against her rules.
Round 3: each row votes to choose one representative, the representatives make the rules, and any row can choose a new representative next week.
(a) Which round shows a monarchy, and which feature tells you so?
(b) Which form of government does Round 2 show?
(c) How many representatives make the rules in Round 3?
(d) In which round can the students change the people who make the rules if they are unhappy, and how?
questions.a: (a) Round 1; the position passes from father to son, and monarchies are usually hereditary. (b) A dictatorship: one person takes absolute power, with no limits on her. (c) 6 representatives, one for each of the 6 rows. (d) Round 3; the students can vote to choose new representatives, as people in a democracy change their representatives through elections.
s: (a) Round 1: hereditary, son takes over from father
(b) Dictatorship
(c) 6 representatives, one per row
(d) Round 3: by voting for new representatives

questions.q:
Ratnapur is a town in a democracy. A citizens' group publishes this record of the last five years.
Fact 1: The richest five families own more than half of the town's land, while 4,000 of its 10,000 households still have no piped water.
Fact 2: 14 of the council's 20 road contracts went, without any open bidding, to firms owned by councillors' families.
Fact 3: For 20 years, the same three families have chaired the town's school board, hospital board and market committee.
Fact 4: In the 2025 council election, half the wards had a single candidate, each a relative of a council member.
(a) Which hurdle to democracy named in the chapter does Fact 1 show?
(b) Which hurdle does Fact 2 show?
(c) Which hurdle does Fact 3 show?
(d) The chapter says elections keep a constant check on what a government does. Which one of the four facts most directly weakens that check? Decide and justify.
(e) Suggest one thing Ratnapur's citizens can do, using the chapter's idea of how people keep a check on government.
questions.a: (a) Wealth disparity. (b) Corruption. (c) Excessive control by a few over democratic institutions. (d) Fact 4: where a ward has only one candidate, the voters cannot change their representative through the election, so the constant check that elections give is lost there; Facts 1-3 are serious but leave the vote itself a real choice. (e) Stay vigilant and use the next election to change their representatives, for example by putting up and voting for other candidates, since elections keep a constant check on what the government does.
s: (a) Wealth disparity
(b) Corruption
(c) Excessive control by a few over democratic institutions
(d) Fact 4, because one candidate means voters cannot change their representative
(e) Use elections to change representatives, staying vigilant
